# Juicy Lucy Loop Dive Bar Guide
Minneapolis, Minnesota
Burn Your Mouth For Burger Bliss
Forgive the title of this dive bar crawl as the alliteration was a bit too irresistible to pass up, much like a Juicy Lucy, or “Jucy Lucy” as we’ll come to discuss. On rare but wonderful occasion, the worlds of dive bar authenticity and tourist destination can overlap. Food tourism in Minneapolis could be built around a lot of the region’s Upper Midwest classics, but the discussion almost universally centers on the Juicy Lucy, a hamburger patty molded to encase a molten cheese center. Done right, and allowed to cool so as not to induce third-degree burns, oozing melty cheese pouring out of a well-cooked burger is pretty hard to beat.
There are two dueling originators of the delicacy, 5-8 Club and Matt’s Bar. The stories conflict, but perhaps the more material difference today is that Matt’s Bar offers a “Jucy Lucy” one way where the 5-8 Club allows for some modification of burger toppings. 5-8 Club feels a bit more like a diner that happens to have a bar in back. Matt’s Bar is a proper dive bar that happens to have a grill in front. The experiences are different, amazing and worth the trip.
But like any great phenomenon, it has not been contained to its originators and countless bars and restaurants offer a juicy hamburger of some variety throughout the city. This is certainly a driving endeavor rather than a walking dive bar crawl, and some serious timing is going to be required to hit them all in any reasonable time period but were our stomachs made of steel and our car at the ready, these are our favorite Juicy Lucy destinations.

A nice evening wandering neighborhood streets is best fueled by at least a little something in one's stomach. These area options fit our divey vibe and will fit into any neighborhood bar crawl.

As far as Juicy Lucy pilgrimages go, there is no wrong answer between starting at either 5-8 Club or Matt’s Bar. The only mistake would be to choose just one. The history and lore of the Juicy Lucy, 5-8 Club, Matt’s and the many televised debates about the better burger are well documented elsewhere.
This is about the atmosphere itself and the 5-8 Club is the larger of the two establishments, offers a full range of food items for those non-Juicy Lucy lovers in your life and, crucially for those visiting, sits only a few minutes from the airport. Booth seating rings an active front room, a small dive bar-like area in back and a handful of servers well-used to steady streams of Lucy seekers. Primary distinction here is the diversity of the menu, where the Juicy Lucy is more a blank canvas that can be shaped and modified in multiple ways to create combinations atop the molten cheese within. Classic location, diner feel, multiple options, more space, that’s 5-8 Club.

# Juicy Lucy Loop Dive Bar Guide
Downtown Minneapolis is a fascinating exercise in urban planning, where the region’s cold weather has prompted the city to adopt a vast network of skyways that allow downtown visitors to traverse great portions of the city without ever stepping foot outside. The phenomenon can sometimes make the city streets feel a little empty in colder weather as pedestrians shelter in the skyways, but the marquee outside Hell’s Kitchen certainly breaks the visual sameness. The restaurant’s independent nature and dive bar-like slogan (“unique but not fancy, interesting but not fussy”) make it interesting. The fact that it sits underground makes it compelling, aided by the presence of the Juicy Lucifer on the menu (get it). Red pepper jelly is the condiment of distinction here, but as downtown dining options go, Hell’s Kitchen provides a unique experience and a Juicy Lucy to boot.

Minneapolis, Minnesota
Burn Your Mouth For Burger Bliss
Forgive the title of this dive bar crawl as the alliteration was a bit too irresistible to pass up, much like a Juicy Lucy, or “Jucy Lucy” as we’ll come to discuss. On rare but wonderful occasion, the worlds of dive bar authenticity and tourist destination can overlap. Food tourism in Minneapolis could be built around a lot of the region’s Upper Midwest classics, but the discussion almost universally centers on the Juicy Lucy, a hamburger patty molded to encase a molten cheese center. Done right, and allowed to cool so as not to induce third-degree burns, oozing melty cheese pouring out of a well-cooked burger is pretty hard to beat.
There are two dueling originators of the delicacy, 5-8 Club and Matt’s Bar. The stories conflict, but perhaps the more material difference today is that Matt’s Bar offers a “Jucy Lucy” one way where the 5-8 Club allows for some modification of burger toppings. 5-8 Club feels a bit more like a diner that happens to have a bar in back. Matt’s Bar is a proper dive bar that happens to have a grill in front. The experiences are different, amazing and worth the trip.
But like any great phenomenon, it has not been contained to its originators and countless bars and restaurants offer a juicy hamburger of some variety throughout the city. This is certainly a driving endeavor rather than a walking dive bar crawl, and some serious timing is going to be required to hit them all in any reasonable time period but were our stomachs made of steel and our car at the ready, these are our favorite Juicy Lucy destinations.

## Urban centers
### Kansas City
See also: Kansas City-style barbecue
Kansas City is an important barbecue and meat-processing center with a distinctive barbecue style. The Kansas City metropolitan area has more than 100 barbecue restaurants46 and proclaims itself to be the "world's barbecue capital."
The Kansas City Barbeque Society47 spreads its influence across the nation through its barbecue-contest standards. Kansas City's barbecue craze can be traced back to Henry Perry, who in the early 1920s started barbecuing in an outdoor pit adjacent to his streetcar barn.48

## Urban centers
### St. Louis
Main article: Cuisine of St. Louis
See also: St. Louis-style barbecue and St. Louis-style pizza
The large number of Irish and German immigrants who came to St. Louis beginning in the early 19th century contributed significantly to the shaping of local cuisine by their uses of beef, pork, and chicken, often roasted or grilled, and desserts including rich cakes, stollens, fruit pies, doughnuts, and cookies. A local form of fresh-stick pretzel, called Gus's Pretzels, has been sold singly and by the bagful by street-corner vendors.
Mayfair salad dressing was a mainstay at a St. Louis hotel of the same name, and one of the original recipes from the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair.49
St. Louis is also known for popularizing the ice cream cone and for inventing gooey butter cake (a rich, soft-centered coffee cake) and frozen custard. Iced tea is also rumored to have been invented at the World's Fair, as well as the hot dog bun.
A staple of grilling in St. Louis is the pork steak, which is sliced from the shoulder of the pig and often basted with or simmered in barbecue sauce during cooking.
Other popular grilled items include crispy snoots, cut from the cheeks and nostrils of the pig; bratwurst; and Italian sausage, often referred to as "sah-zittsa," a localization of its Italian name, _salsiccia_. Maull's is a popular brand of barbecue sauce in the St. Louis area.
Restaurants on The Hill reflect the lasting influence of the early 20th-century Milanese and Sicilian immigrant community. Two unique Italian-American style dishes include "toasted" ravioli, which is breaded and fried, and St. Louis-style pizza, which has a crisp, thin crust and is usually made with Provel cheese instead of traditional mozzarella.
A poor boy sandwich is the traditional name in St. Louis for a submarine sandwich. A St. Paul sandwich is a St. Louis sandwich, available in Chinese-American restaurants. A slinger is a diner and late-night specialty consisting of eggs, hash browns, and hamburger, topped with chili, cheese, and onion.

## Urban centers
### Milwaukee
Traditional cuisine in Wisconsin was influenced by the European immigration there, so much, that it could be considered the "most European in the United States".50 Foods frequently considered comfort foods, and foods signature to Wisconsin culture in Milwaukee include cheese dishes, butter burgers, beer, Bloody Marys, beer soup, cheese curds, fish fry, and bratwursts.515253 There is a sizeable number of farms spread across Wisconsin for dairy, corn, and meat production.5455

## Urban centers
### Twin Cities of Minnesota
Main article: Cuisine of Minnesota
Once known as "Mill City", homemade breads and pies feature prominently in Minneapolis cuisine.56 Bread and cakes available at the Eagle Bakery in 1850 included fruitcake, pound cake and something called "Fancy cake" for the holidays. In the 1930s, there were four Jewish bakeries within a few blocks of each other baking bagels and other fresh breads. Jewish families purchased _challah_ loaves for their Sabbath meal at the North Side Bakery. There were two kosher meat markets and four Jewish delicatessens, one of which began distribution for what would become Sara Lee frozen cheesecakes. The delis sold sandwiches like corned beef and salami.57
Minneapolis is more racially and ethnically diverse than the rest of Minnesota. For the diverse ethnic groups that call Minneapolis home, retaining their distinct ethnic culture remains a goal that is supported by ethnic-oriented community organizations. Celebrating ethnic holidays and get togethers by preparing traditional foods remains a major symbol of cultural retention. It is a way people share their heritage and culture with outsiders. There are a plethora of restaurants serving ethnic cuisines.58
Today, there are many restaurants serving various Polish dishes like polish sausage, pierogies and stuffed cabbage rolls.59 and typical German foods like _rippchen_, _knackwurst_, and _wiener schnitzel_. Traditionally, potato salad and kraut were served alongside an entree of bratwurst or ham hocks. A side of _spaetzle_ and red cabbage would accompany _sauerbraten_ or _rouladen_.60
In the fall, the Twin Cities share along with Green Bay, Wisconsin, the tradition of the neighborhood booyah, a cuisine and cultural event featuring a hodge-podge of ingredients in stews.61
American restaurants in the Twin Cities supply a wide spectrum of choices and styles that range from small diners, sports bars and decades-old supper clubs to high-end steakhouses and eateries that serve new American cuisine using locally grown ingredients. The Jucy Lucy (or "Juicy Lucy"), claimed as an innovation of the local pubs, is a hamburger with a core of melted cheese.62Barbecue restaurants in the area tend to feature a combination of the various regional styles of this type of cooking.

## Urban centers
### Twin Cities of Minnesota
Minneapolis and St. Paul also offer a diverse array of cuisines influenced by their many immigrant groups. In the 1970s the Twin Cities saw a large influx of Southeast Asian immigrants from Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Asian cuisine was initially dominated by Chinese Cantonese immigrants that served Americanized offerings. In 1883 Woo Yee Sing and his younger brother, Woo Du Sing, opened the Canton Cafe in Minneapolis, the first Chinese restaurant in Minnesota.6364 Authentic offerings began at the influential Nankin Cafe which opened in 1919,65 and many new Chinese immigrants soon took this cuisine throughout the Twin Cities and to the suburbs. The cuisine of Japan has been present since the opening of the area's very first Japanese restaurant, Fuji Ya in 1959.66 Since 1976 Supenn Supatanskinkasem has been cooking and serving Thai food through her Minnesota State Fair Booth, Siam Café, and Sawatdee chain of Thai restaurants.67 Modern dining options include _phở_ noodle shops, _banh mi_ and Thai curry restaurants.
Restaurants offering other cuisines of Asia including those from Afghanistan, India, Nepal and the Philippines are also recent additions to the Twin Cities dining scene. Local ingredients are often integrated into Asian offerings, for example Chinese steamed walleye and Nepalese curried bison.
Mexican and Tex-Mex restaurants serve _tacos_, _tortas_, _tamales_ and other similar dishes. Cuisines from Argentina, Brazil, Cuba, Ecuador, Peru and the Spanish Speaking West Indies are also represented,68 as well as Native American cuisine.6970
The Twin Cities are home to many restaurants that serve the cuisines of the Mediterranean, Middle East and Northeast Africa including, Greek,71Ethiopian and Somalia have also opened a number of restaurants in Minnesota.72
West-African immigrants have brought their own cuisine in recent years. There is also a presence of Afro-Caribbean restaurants, with the famed Nicollet Avenue in Minneapolis being home to two Caribbean restaurants.73

## Urban centers
### Omaha
Main article: Cuisine of Omaha
Omaha is known for its steakhouses, many of which have closed.74
Central European and Southern influences can be seen in the local popularity of carp and South 24th Street contains a multitude of Mexican restaurants. North Omaha also has its own barbecue style.
Omaha is one of the places claiming to have invented the reuben sandwich, supposedly named for Reuben Kulakofsky, a grocer from the Dundee neighborhood.75
Godfather's Pizza is one of the chain restaurants that originated in Omaha.76
The cheese frenchee is also a local favorite and staple, originating from the original King's Food Host fast-food restaurants.77

## Urban centers
### Kansas City
See also: Kansas City-style barbecue
Kansas City is an important barbecue and meat-processing center with a distinctive barbecue style. The Kansas City metropolitan area has more than 100 barbecue restaurants46 and proclaims itself to be the "world's barbecue capital."
The Kansas City Barbeque Society47 spreads its influence across the nation through its barbecue-contest standards. Kansas City's barbecue craze can be traced back to Henry Perry, who in the early 1920s started barbecuing in an outdoor pit adjacent to his streetcar barn.48
texts.12:
## Urban centers
### St. Louis
Main article: Cuisine of St. Louis
See also: St. Louis-style barbecue and St. Louis-style pizza
The large number of Irish and German immigrants who came to St. Louis beginning in the early 19th century contributed significantly to the shaping of local cuisine by their uses of beef, pork, and chicken, often roasted or grilled, and desserts including rich cakes, stollens, fruit pies, doughnuts, and cookies. A local form of fresh-stick pretzel, called Gus's Pretzels, has been sold singly and by the bagful by street-corner vendors.
Mayfair salad dressing was a mainstay at a St. Louis hotel of the same name, and one of the original recipes from the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair.49
St. Louis is also known for popularizing the ice cream cone and for inventing gooey butter cake (a rich, soft-centered coffee cake) and frozen custard. Iced tea is also rumored to have been invented at the World's Fair, as well as the hot dog bun.
A staple of grilling in St. Louis is the pork steak, which is sliced from the shoulder of the pig and often basted with or simmered in barbecue sauce during cooking.
Other popular grilled items include crispy snoots, cut from the cheeks and nostrils of the pig; bratwurst; and Italian sausage, often referred to as "sah-zittsa," a localization of its Italian name, _salsiccia_. Maull's is a popular brand of barbecue sauce in the St. Louis area.
Restaurants on The Hill reflect the lasting influence of the early 20th-century Milanese and Sicilian immigrant community. Two unique Italian-American style dishes include "toasted" ravioli, which is breaded and fried, and St. Louis-style pizza, which has a crisp, thin crust and is usually made with Provel cheese instead of traditional mozzarella.
A poor boy sandwich is the traditional name in St. Louis for a submarine sandwich. A St. Paul sandwich is a St. Louis sandwich, available in Chinese-American restaurants. A slinger is a diner and late-night specialty consisting of eggs, hash browns, and hamburger, topped with chili, cheese, and onion.

### Milwaukee
Traditional cuisine in Wisconsin was influenced by the European immigration there, so much, that it could be considered the "most European in the United States".50 Foods frequently considered comfort foods, and foods signature to Wisconsin culture in Milwaukee include cheese dishes, butter burgers, beer, Bloody Marys, beer soup, cheese curds, fish fry, and bratwursts.515253 There is a sizeable number of farms spread across Wisconsin for dairy, corn, and meat production.5455

## Urban centers
### Twin Cities of Minnesota
Main article: Cuisine of Minnesota
Once known as "Mill City", homemade breads and pies feature prominently in Minneapolis cuisine.56 Bread and cakes available at the Eagle Bakery in 1850 included fruitcake, pound cake and something called "Fancy cake" for the holidays. In the 1930s, there were four Jewish bakeries within a few blocks of each other baking bagels and other fresh breads. Jewish families purchased _challah_ loaves for their Sabbath meal at the North Side Bakery. There were two kosher meat markets and four Jewish delicatessens, one of which began distribution for what would become Sara Lee frozen cheesecakes. The delis sold sandwiches like corned beef and salami.57
Minneapolis is more racially and ethnically diverse than the rest of Minnesota. For the diverse ethnic groups that call Minneapolis home, retaining their distinct ethnic culture remains a goal that is supported by ethnic-oriented community organizations. Celebrating ethnic holidays and get togethers by preparing traditional foods remains a major symbol of cultural retention. It is a way people share their heritage and culture with outsiders. There are a plethora of restaurants serving ethnic cuisines.58
Today, there are many restaurants serving various Polish dishes like polish sausage, pierogies and stuffed cabbage rolls.59 and typical German foods like _rippchen_, _knackwurst_, and _wiener schnitzel_. Traditionally, potato salad and kraut were served alongside an entree of bratwurst or ham hocks. A side of _spaetzle_ and red cabbage would accompany _sauerbraten_ or _rouladen_.60
In the fall, the Twin Cities share along with Green Bay, Wisconsin, the tradition of the neighborhood booyah, a cuisine and cultural event featuring a hodge-podge of ingredients in stews.61
American restaurants in the Twin Cities supply a wide spectrum of choices and styles that range from small diners, sports bars and decades-old supper clubs to high-end steakhouses and eateries that serve new American cuisine using locally grown ingredients. The Jucy Lucy (or "Juicy Lucy"), claimed as an innovation of the local pubs, is a hamburger with a core of melted cheese.62Barbecue restaurants in the area tend to feature a combination of the various regional styles of this type of cooking.

## Urban centers
### Twin Cities of Minnesota
Minneapolis and St. Paul also offer a diverse array of cuisines influenced by their many immigrant groups. In the 1970s the Twin Cities saw a large influx of Southeast Asian immigrants from Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Asian cuisine was initially dominated by Chinese Cantonese immigrants that served Americanized offerings. In 1883 Woo Yee Sing and his younger brother, Woo Du Sing, opened the Canton Cafe in Minneapolis, the first Chinese restaurant in Minnesota.6364 Authentic offerings began at the influential Nankin Cafe which opened in 1919,65 and many new Chinese immigrants soon took this cuisine throughout the Twin Cities and to the suburbs. The cuisine of Japan has been present since the opening of the area's very first Japanese restaurant, Fuji Ya in 1959.66 Since 1976 Supenn Supatanskinkasem has been cooking and serving Thai food through her Minnesota State Fair Booth, Siam Café, and Sawatdee chain of Thai restaurants.67 Modern dining options include _phở_ noodle shops, _banh mi_ and Thai curry restaurants.
Restaurants offering other cuisines of Asia including those from Afghanistan, India, Nepal and the Philippines are also recent additions to the Twin Cities dining scene. Local ingredients are often integrated into Asian offerings, for example Chinese steamed walleye and Nepalese curried bison.
Mexican and Tex-Mex restaurants serve _tacos_, _tortas_, _tamales_ and other similar dishes. Cuisines from Argentina, Brazil, Cuba, Ecuador, Peru and the Spanish Speaking West Indies are also represented,68 as well as Native American cuisine.6970
The Twin Cities are home to many restaurants that serve the cuisines of the Mediterranean, Middle East and Northeast Africa including, Greek,71Ethiopian and Somalia have also opened a number of restaurants in Minnesota.72
West-African immigrants have brought their own cuisine in recent years. There is also a presence of Afro-Caribbean restaurants, with the famed Nicollet Avenue in Minneapolis being home to two Caribbean restaurants.73

Main article: Cuisine of Omaha
Omaha is known for its steakhouses, many of which have closed.74
Central European and Southern influences can be seen in the local popularity of carp and South 24th Street contains a multitude of Mexican restaurants. North Omaha also has its own barbecue style.
Omaha is one of the places claiming to have invented the reuben sandwich, supposedly named for Reuben Kulakofsky, a grocer from the Dundee neighborhood.75
Godfather's Pizza is one of the chain restaurants that originated in Omaha.76
The cheese frenchee is also a local favorite and staple, originating from the original King's Food Host fast-food restaurants.77

### J. Miller Steak Company
Family-owned and operated steakhouse in historic two-story brick building on scenic Route 56, featuring wood-fired grills and affordable menu options for the whole family. Open-concept seating with exposed brick walls, high ceilings, and vintage-inspired lighting creates comfortable yet special atmosphere. Live local musicians on Friday nights. Wood-fired steaks including ribeye, filet, and salmon served in intimate dining room with purple upholstered chairs. Established 2020.
$$$

### Jag's Steak & Seafood
Opened in 2003 as West Chester’s first fine-dining restaurant, Jag’s Steak & Seafood was built on a partnership between founder John Allgaier and Chef Michelle Brown, who later became chef proprietor and majority owner. The menu blends classic steakhouse traditions with contemporary touches, complemented by a deep wine cellar and a polished raw bar. Beyond the dining room, live music in the piano bar has helped establish Jag’s as a full evening destination, pairing refined food with entertainment and an enduring local reputation.
$$$$

### Legend's Cocktail Lounge
A downtown Broadway storefront that Miami County locals will tell you serves the best steak around, wrapped wall to wall in a music-legends theme: pop-art icons, gold cherubs and columns, a motorcycle parked indoors, and a stage built into the dining room for live bands. The cocktail list runs on the same conceit, every drink a riff on a music or pop-culture figure, and regulars name their bartender in reviews. Past the steaks the kitchen turns out breaded tenderloins, loaded burgers, a house barbecue sauce on half the menu, and a torched crème brûlée cheesecake.
$$

### Libby's Southern Comfort
Named for owner Brad Wainscott's daughter and family black lab, Libby's Southern Comfort brings award-winning Southern cuisine to Covington's Duveneck Square in a restored industrial space that's home to the original Cheerwine Bourbon Slush. With goetta hush puppies made from Glier's Goetta, special-recipe fried chicken with hot honey, fresh oysters shucked to order, and fried green tomatoes piled with pimento cheese and bourbon onion jam, this family-founded casual eatery pairs comfort food at its best with a vintage bourbon collection and rotating specialty slushes on a year-round dog-friendly patio where "come as you are" isn't just a vibe—it's a promise, with all bread from Sixteen Bricks and oatmeal cream pies that beat Little Debbie every time.
$$

### MRBL
Northern Kentucky's premiere dining destination combining exceptional steakhouse classics with authentic sushi and innovative seafood creations in an aesthetic masterpiece setting overlooking the Ohio River to downtown Cincinnati. Features prime dry-aged beef from Chicago alongside an authentic sushi menu and weekly fresh seafood specials, delivering a truly unique fine dining experience that seamlessly blends steakhouse traditions with Japanese culinary artistry.
$$$$

### Maury's Tiny Cove
Established in 1949, this longtime Cincinnati steakhouse feels like a step back into a mid-century speakeasy, complete with low lighting, classic booths, and old-school charm. The menu remains rooted in tradition, featuring char-grilled steaks, seafood, and legacy dishes that have defined the restaurant for decades. With its iconic dancing bull sign still welcoming guests and a legacy tied to classic cocktails, Rat Pack lore, and even film history, it remains a place where nostalgia and a good night out go hand in hand.
$$$

### Noche
From the team behind Alfio's Buon Cibo (OpenTable's Top 100 in America), Noche blends Italian tradition with Argentine passion in a moody, magnetic space built for late-night energy and shared plates. Chef Alfio Gulisano's fire-kissed menu features house-made pastas, wood-fired creations like empanadas and arancini, and standout dishes like short rib gnocchi, with craft cocktails and an adventurous wine list designed to keep you lingering long after dinner.
$$$

### Pompilios
Historic Italian restaurant and bar established in 1933 in a building dating to 1902, serving generations with Mrs. Pompilio's homemade ravioli recipe, Italian sausage, lasagna, cannelloni, and traditional pastas in Newport's legendary corner location. Featured in Rain Man (1988) with Dustin Hoffman and Tom Cruise, boasting regulation bocce courts with 64-team league, live music several nights weekly, Kentucky bourbon collection on the original back bar, and over a century of stories including mobsters, celebrities like Frank Sinatra and Marilyn Monroe, and families bringing second and third generations to this Italian restaurant with Kentucky flavor and unparalleled hospitality.
$$

### Prairie Grass Café
Opened in 2004 by chefs Sarah Stegner and George Bumbaris, longtime colleagues at the Ritz-Carlton Chicago. Stegner is a two-time James Beard Award winner, and the pair chose a stretch of Skokie Boulevard over downtown, building a relaxed, upscale neighborhood room around seasonal American cooking. The menu shifts with the harvest, drawing on local farms and Chicago’s Green City Market. The bunless 10-ounce sirloin burger, once named Chicago’s best, is the signature, alongside Finn’s Ranch deviled eggs. A thoughtful cocktail menu, a deep wine list and a private dining room round out the experience.
$$$

### Prime Cincinnati
An upscale steakhouse and seafood restaurant built around meticulous execution, attentive service, and a deep respect for premium ingredients. Led by Chef Shawn Heine, the menu highlights prime steaks, fresh seafood, and thoughtful preparations designed to balance refinement with approachability. A robust wine program plays a central role in the experience, complemented by a polished lounge featuring handcrafted cocktails, a cigar patio, and rotating midweek specials. The overall atmosphere feels confident and composed, making it a natural choice for celebratory dinners, business meals, or an elevated evening out downtown.
$$$

### Purple Poulet
Named Best Fried Chicken in Kentucky by Southern Living, this Southern Bourbon Bistro features over 550 bourbons, ryes, and whiskeys with farm-fresh ingredients and classic southern cooking inspired by Charleston and New Orleans with Kentucky infusion. Five dining rooms including main floor and four upstairs spaces, plus a hidden speakeasy-style "Gangster" party room behind a secret door paying homage to Newport's "Sin City" history, delivering unparalleled southern culture, hospitality, and flavors of the Bluegrass State and Deep South.
$$$$

### Ripple Wine Bar & Restaurant
Thoughtfully designed wine bar and restaurant with locations in Covington, Kentucky and Cincinnati, Ohio, offering the largest selection of wine by the glass in Northern Kentucky and Cincinnati with a rotating collection from across the globe. Features seasonal favorites, timeless classics, and boutique hard-to-finds served alongside wine-friendly snacks and petite entrees that change with the seasons, all delivered by friendly, knowledgeable staff passionate about wine and perfect pairings.
$$$

### Sanctuary Social
A vibrant vibe. Sanctuary Social is a warm, inviting gathering place designed for friends, families, and neighbors to connect over shareable plates, craft cocktails, curated wines, and thoughtful pairings that encourage conversation. Beyond the dining experience, Sanctuary Social hosts exclusive club events, chef-inspired dinners, and community gatherings that make each visit feel both personal and memorable.
$$

### Sweet Basil Thai & Sushi
Locally owned since 2006, Sweet Basil has been Northern Kentucky's quiet answer to authentic Thai and fresh sushi for nearly two decades — tucked into a Crescent Springs strip while the chains around it cycle in and out. Family-run, independently owned, one location. The kitchen does Thai classics and sushi under the same roof, with a heat scale that actually means something. Carry-out is efficient. Dine-in gives you the full picture.
$$

### Thai Pavilion
Opened in October 2023 by three women united by their love of Thai food and culture—Anya Hoffman, Wun Woon, and head chef Premmy—Thai Pavilion brings authentic Thai cuisine to Covington's Scott Street. The restaurant serves traditional dishes like pad thai, red curry, pad kee mao (drunken noodles), khao soi, and massaman curry, with customizable spice levels that can satisfy everyone from mild preferences to "thermonuclear" authentic Thai heat. Named after the Thai cultural concept of pavilions as community gathering places, the restaurant has quickly become a downtown lunch favorite for neighboring office workers and a destination for Northern Kentucky foodies seeking genuine Thai flavors.
$$

### The Rathskeller
Indianapolis' oldest restaurant, serving continuously since 1894 from the cellar of the Athenaeum, the German Renaissance Revival landmark built as Das Deutsche Haus and designed by the firm of Bernard Vonnegut, grandfather of Kurt. The dining room is beamed and paneled, hung with steins and painted German proverbs, with a brick corridor of mounted game and state coats of arms leading to the Kellerbar. The kitchen still cooks the old menu: rouladen, schnitzel, sauerbraten, oxtail soup, house sauerkraut, alongside steaks and seafood. Twelve imported drafts, fifty-plus imported bottles, and live music most nights in the biergarten.
$$$

### Beehive Augusta Tavern
Historic farm-to-table restaurant in a 1796 building on the banks of the Ohio River, constructed on land granted to a Revolutionary War veteran and listed on the National Registry of Historic Sites. The building survived being set on fire during the 1862 Battle of Augusta and the Great Flood of 1937, serving over the centuries as a residence, general store, pharmacy, and ferry office with views of the still-operating Augusta Ferry. Reopened in 2017 by Lance and Lalani Bates, featuring seasonal menus with locally sourced ingredients, extensive bourbon selection, craft cocktails, rustic dining room with hive-shaped lighting, second-floor river-view balcony, weekend brunch, and live entertainment, serving signature dishes including Kentucky Hot Brown, charcuterie boards, filet, pork chops, and the Beehive Burger.
$$$

### Bella Roma
Small, family-owned Italian restaurant in downtown New Albany since 2010. All pasta and sauces made from scratch daily—demand often exceeds supply, with certain dishes selling out by evening's end. Classic Italian menu done right: veal parmigiana, chicken saltimbocca, chicken piccata, and house-made cannoli and gelato. Intimate dining room adds to the charm, making guests feel like they've stepped into an Italian family kitchen. Warm bread served with true marinara. BYOB-friendly atmosphere with outdoor sidewalk seating available.
$$
A scratch Italian kitchen with roots going back to 2010 in downtown New Albany — where it operated first as Connor's Place, then La Bocca, then Bella Roma beginning in 2014. Recently relocated to the Jeffersonville riverfront, it brought its following with it. All pasta and sauces made fresh daily; when dishes sell out, they're gone. The menu is classic Italian-American without shortcuts: veal parmigiana, chicken piccata, chicken saltimbocca, seafood linguini, tiramisu, and housemade cannoli. Small room, intimate feel.
$$

### Bender's Pub Grub
Bender's Pub Grub operates out of Alexandria Brewing Company, but make no mistake — this is chef Shawn Weinbender's show. The menu is scratch-made southern comfort food that regularly surprises people who showed up expecting bar snacks. The smoked wings with house-made Alabama White sauce have their own following, and the chicken and waffles and shrimp and grits get mentioned in the same breath as the best versions in the area. $6 Wing Wednesdays keep the regulars coming. Live music, a full craft beer tap list from Alexandria Brewing, and a backroom with arcade games and pinball round out the experience. The kind of place you stumble into for a beer and leave wondering why you waited so long.
$$

### Berd's Grill & Bar
Local sports bar opened June 2019 by Matt Berding (Badin High School 2000) and Robert MacKendrick (Fairfield High School 1999) in the Village Green development. The space previously housed Symmes Tavern and Roc's Grill & Bar—Berd's honors the legacy with "Symmes Tavern Ribs" on the menu. Focused on being a community gathering place with high-quality bar food: wings, homemade pizza, burgers, sandwiches, and apps like cheese moons and egg rolls. The tap list features local craft from Municipal and Fretboard alongside domestic staples. Features a spacious patio, private event room ("Berd's Nest" for up to 50 guests), and TVs throughout for game day.
$$

### Black Olive Italian Restaurant
Situated on Madison's hilltop, this is one of the few full-service Italian kitchens in the region south of Corydon. The menu draws from traditional Italian-American staples — eggplant parmigiana, veal parmigiana, puttanesca, chicken gnocchi, manicotti, seafood linguini — with homemade marinara and complimentary seasoned bread on arrival. Open daily for lunch and dinner. The kitchen leans on fresh, market-sourced ingredients; portions are generous. A full bar, outdoor seating, and a relaxed atmosphere make it a viable anchor for the Madison dining scene.
$$

### Blue Ash Chili - Blue Ash
Not your typical Cincinnati chili parlor. Since 1969, Blue Ash Chili has made its premium chili using the same family recipe with top-quality ingredients—not too spicy, served Cincy-style from cheese coneys up to 6-ways with fresh jalapeños and fried bottle caps. The small-town diner feel keeps regulars coming back, but it's the famous double-deckers, hearty breakfasts, and creative menu that set it apart. Featured on Guy Fieri's "Diners, Drive-Ins & Dives" in 2010, it was also named Official Chili of the WEBN Fireworks + Cincinnati Riverfest that same year.
$

### Bones' Burgers
Owner Curtis Bonekemper — “Bones” — spent six years building a following via food truck before opening this Montgomery brick-and-mortar. The commitment carried over: 100% grass-fed and finished Black Angus beef, local sourcing, and careful cooking. Patties come in quarter, third, or half-pound sizes with specialty builds or full customization. A vegan burger and salmon burger round out the menu for non-beef eaters. Cozy space (48 capacity max) with a good beer and wine selection. The Oakley second location has since closed; this is the one.
$$

### Boomtown Biscuits & Whiskey
Boomtown Biscuits & Whiskey brings modern American frontier cooking to Union, Kentucky, where Chef Christian Gill (a Guy's Grocery Games winner) crafts made-from-scratch biscuits using his grandmother's recipe alongside bold dishes like the Mother Load, Rhine Poutine, and their signature fried chicken biscuit. This restaurant pairs comfort food with bourbon and whiskey in a casual atmosphere, serving breakfast and lunch Wednesday through Sunday. Boomtown offers a taste of Southern hospitality with creative twists on classic comfort dishes.
$$

### Boonedocks Pub and Grub
Boonedocks Pub and Grub serves New American pub fare near Big Bone Lick State Park in Union, offering hand-patted burgers, smoked ribs, beer cheese pretzels, and NY strip steaks in a sports bar atmosphere with 12 beers on draft and 80" TVs. The dog-friendly patio and live music on weekends make it a local gathering spot for catching the game or unwinding with good food and drinks.
$$

### Boscoe's Place
Craft pizzas, smashed burgers, wings, and sandwiches in a pub-style atmosphere. Named in memory of owners' longtime canine companion. Buffalo chicken and BBQ Dad Bod pizzas are local favorites. Dog-friendly outdoor patio. Consistently praised for cleanliness, friendly service, and "big city vibe" in small-town Covington.
$$

### Bourbon House Pizza - Newport
The Newport half of a Northern Kentucky family pizza business that started in Florence in 2007. Owner Mary Brandstetter runs this shop with her son Jeremy, while her daughter Stephanie runs the original. The draw is Chicago-style deep dish built on dough and sauce made fresh every day, with thin crust, hoagies, calzones and appetizers rounding out the menu. Wine and bourbon are on hand for the grown-ups. It sits on Aqua Way near Newport on the Levee, which makes it an easy stop before or after a day on the riverfront.
$$

### Bow Tie Café
Founded 2010 by former Cincinnati Bengal Dhani Jones, Caveh Azadeh, and NiKo Grammas. Named for friend Kunta Littlejohn who said "If you wanna be somebody, you gotta rock a bow tie"—when Kunta was diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, they created Bow Tie Cause supporting Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. Managing Partner Heather Turner (Mt. Adams resident) joined 2013. Only café in Cincinnati pouring Intelligentsia coffee daily. Fresh Sixteen Bricks bread. Casual bistro fare—breakfast, lunch, weekend brunch. Three-tier patio is dog friendly. Coffee-inspired craft cocktails. Steps from Eden Park, Art Museum, and Playhouse.
$$

### BrewRiver Creole Kitchen
New Orleans-inspired Creole gastropub from owner Joby Bowman and Chef Michael Shields, established 2012. Relocated 2018 to expand kitchen and focus on authentic Creole cuisine. Scratch-made menu features 12-hour dark roux Chicken & Sausage Gumbo, Pasta Monica, Alligator and Waffle, Fried Green Tomatoes, Jambalaya, and Bananas Foster Bread Pudding. Twenty-three craft beers on tap, craft cocktails. Live music featuring blues and boogie-woogie piano. Sunday brunch with performances. Outdoor garden room, private event space for up to 100. BrewRiver Stein Club membership available.
$$

### Broken Barrel Bar & Grill
Brian and Tracy Teetzen had so much fun building The Cracked Pot that they knew they had more to offer. Their second restaurant, just a few blocks down Central Avenue, lets these two restaurateurs—who met as teenagers working in a restaurant—bring in recipes inspired by their travels and Midwest roots.
$$

### Lucky's Taproom & Eatery
Oregon District neighborhood spot established in 2011 by owner Andrew Trick, who brings over 30 years in the hospitality industry. The real standout: dedicated dual flat-top grills ensure true vegan and vegetarian dishes never touch meat—a rarity in pub dining. Twenty revolving craft beer taps offer the largest draft selection in the Oregon District, with new selections rotating regularly. Homemade soups, weekly specials, and scratch desserts complement traditional pub fare. Model cars line the walls, TVs broadcast games, and the atmosphere stays comfortable and unpretentious. Weekend brunch served Saturday and Sunday.
$$

### Ludlow Bromley Yacht Club
Ludlow Bromley Yacht Club brings beach vibes to the Ohio River from its floating barges in Ludlow, serving pub classics like grouper sandwiches and cold drinks alongside live music and man-made beach seating. Owners Steve and Andrea Gott rebuilt this iconic NKY landmark after a barge destroyed it in 2019, reopening in 2025 with the same cash-only, laid-back river atmosphere that made it a community gathering spot for nearly three decades. With its marina docking and waterfront location, LBYC is where Northern Kentucky meets summer vacation—no matter the season.
$$

### MVP Sports Bar & Grille
Family-owned sports bar in Silverton's heart, dedicated to a casual atmosphere with diverse menu and drink selection. Burgers, wings, famous box tots, flatbread pizzas, and daily specials satisfy every craving. Twelve tap handles focus on local craft brews alongside domestics, imports, and a full bar. Large patio, private party room, live music, and free trivia Thursdays make it a neighborhood gathering spot for food, fun, and entertainment.
$$

### MaanKi Thali
Authentic Gujarati restaurant founded in 2020, bringing homestyle Indian cuisine to Mason. Traditional copper thalis served with multiple curries, dal, rice, roti, puri, farsan, sweet, and chhas (spiced buttermilk). Rotating specials include Kathiyawadi thali (Friday) and Gujarati thali. Also offers Indian street food like sev usal, paneer bhurji, and methi pakoda. Catering available. Near Kings Island and Deerfield Towne Center.
$$

### MadTree Parks & Rec
MadTree's boldest venture yet opened February 2025 inside a renovated 15,000-square-foot airplane hangar at Summit Park. Co-founded in 2013 by Brady Duncan, Jeff Hunt, and Kenny McNutt, MadTree built its reputation on award-winning craft beers and a deep commitment to sustainability—they're Ohio's only B Corp-certified brewery. Parks & Rec was designed for families and outdoor lovers, featuring indoor and outdoor kids' play areas, all-day brunch, wood-fired pizzas, and a patio that seamlessly blends into the park's green space. The "Branch Out" program makes this one of the region's most inclusive restaurants for guests with developmental disabilities, complete with a calming room developed alongside Cincinnati Children's Hospital.
$$

### Mae Ploy's Thai Restaurant
Family-owned Thai restaurant in Lebanon's historic downtown, housed in a converted bank building where the original vault remains visible. Owner Nuploy ("Mae Ploy") personally greets guests, representing Thailand's "Land of Smiles" philosophy. Authentic traditional dishes include curries, street noodles beyond standard pad Thai, and stir-fry specialties. Full sushi bar with fresh rolls. Opened April 2019 by Ploy and Roy, who transformed a 3,000 sq ft first-floor space into their dream restaurant.
$$

### Main Street Diner
Farm-to-table diner on historic Main Street using all local products with no frozen foods, owned by welcoming operators who source ingredients locally. Breakfast, burgers, barbecue including Tina's Famous BBQ pulled pork sandwich, chili cheese fries, mushroom omelette, biscuits and gravy, and Swiss burgers. Also source for all-natural free-range, grass-fed, pasture-raised beef by the pound. Cozy, quaint atmosphere with outdoor tables and interior reflecting owner's interests. Dine-in, carry-out, and local delivery. Ranked #1 restaurant in Rising Sun.
$

### Maki Mono Covington
Under new ownership since August 2024, this female-owned sushi and sake bar features Executive Chef Roberto Castaneda's pan-Asian kitchen alongside Sushi Chef Isaiah Barrett's creative specialty rolls. The menu spans traditional Japanese offerings like miso soup and fresh sushi to crowd-pleasers like pork dumplings and chicken katsu, paired with an extensive sake selection of 20+ varieties. The cozy cocktail bar atmosphere and friendly service have made this Madison Avenue spot a go-to for both quick lunches and date nights.
$$

### Mansion Hill Tavern
Greater Cincinnati's oldest live music venue, housed in an 1875 building in Newport's East Row Historic District that's served as a café since 1944 and legendary home of the mid-century "boogie woogie" movement with greats like H-Bomb Ferguson and Big Joe Duskin. Now operated by Brian Conner, featuring live blues music every night, home of the Mansion Hill Blues Festival, and serving southern-inspired tavern fare including burgers, Nashville Hot sandwich, fried green tomatoes, fried okra, and award-winning fried chicken. Open daily with lunch, weekend brunch, craft cocktails, and an authentic neighborhood blues atmosphere where "you're only a stranger once."
$

### Marigold
English-style public house fusing British sophistication with bold Indian flavors in a moody Arts and Crafts-inspired setting. Chef Megan Yung (Le Cordon Bleu London-trained) crafts London-style curries like butter chicken and Malabar shrimp with maximized richness, plus charred meats, Scotch eggs, and ale-steamed mussels. Pot pies, fish and chips, and the Marigold burger (Welsh rarebit on house-made English muffin) balance familiar comfort with unexpected spice. Bespoke Cincinnati Distilling gin stars in the signature Pimm's Royal Cup. Deep emerald and crimson tones, antique china place settings, and botanical motifs create sultry, intimate ambiance perfect for adventurous date nights.
$$$

### Market Street Grille
Scratch kitchen restaurant anchoring historic downtown Harrison in beautifully restored mid-1800s Odd Fellows Building. Three siblings purchased and renovated the landmark structure in 1996, earning the 2000 Preservation Award from Cincinnati Preservation Association for excellence in rehabilitation. Familiar homemade dishes using fresh ingredients create nostalgic flavors in relaxed, vintage atmosphere. Menu features Maryland crab cakes, hand-cut Certified Angus Beef burgers, fresh seafood, specialty sandwiches, and impressive salad variety. Weekend prime rib special available while supplies last. Sunday brunch showcases signature potato soup, voted guests' number one choice. Pub-style bar serves upscale liquors and craft brews. Live music and special tasting events pair wine with seasonal menus. Multiple dining rooms accommodate private parties and corporate gatherings with personalized custom menus. Owners Katie and Paul maintain hands-on presence ensuring warm, family-like hospitality.
$$

### Matt the Miller's Tavern Steakhouse
An upscale American tavern and steakhouse built around the idea of craic — an Irish sense of energy, community, and togetherness that shapes the experience from the moment you walk in. The chef-driven menu elevates classic tavern favorites with thoughtful twists, balancing comfort and polish across steaks, entrées, and shareable plates. The atmosphere feels lively and welcoming, making it a natural fit for group gatherings, celebrations, and nights that linger longer than planned.
$$$

### Mayan Cafe
Chef Bruce Ucán, a Mayan Indian from Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, was a pioneer in NuLu when he opened his first restaurant here in 1997. Since 2007, he and co-owner Anne Shadle have served authentic Mayan cuisine using locally-sourced ingredients from Kentucky farms. Their commitment to farm-to-table extends to sustainably produced meats and seasonal produce. Signature dishes include cochinita pibil, mole, and their legendary lima beans. An intimate space with photos of Chef Bruce's village lining the walls.
$$

### Mazunte Taqueria
Oaxacan-inspired taqueria founded by Josh Wamsley after 10 months living and learning to cook in Mexico. Street-style tacos with fresh corn tortillas made in-house—pork with avocado salsa, steak with pickled onion and goat cheese, fish, veggie. Homemade salsa bar with pico, salsa verde, salsa picante. Also enchiladas, quesadillas, pozole, elote. Gluten-free and vegan-friendly. Counter-service with indoor/outdoor seating. Started 2012, now a Cincinnati institution.
$$

### McCollum's on York Closed Permanently
Cozy neighborhood restaurant in the heart of Newport offering a diverse scratch kitchen menu in a warm, welcoming atmosphere with friendly staff. Perfect for leisurely dinners with loved ones, quick lunch catch-ups with friends, or solo meals at the bar, where laughter flows freely and guests are invited to come as they are and leave with satisfied hearts, full stomachs, and smiles.
$$$$

### Selena's at Willow Lake Tavern
A Creole-Sicilian fusion restaurant housed in the legendary Willow Lake Tavern building in Anchorage. Owner Alan Salmon drew on 25 years of running the original Selena's in Tampa—named after Selena Giacona, the matriarch whose recipes inspired the kitchen—and brought the concept to Louisville. Fresh seafood is flown in daily from the East Coast, anchoring a menu of po'boys, gumbo, jambalaya, étouffée, stuffed shrimp, and Sicilian pastas. The outdoor courtyard with a koi pond and the signature beignets at Saturday and Sunday brunch are local favorites.
$$

### Senate - Blue Ash
Gourmet hot dog and gastropub from Queen City Hospitality Group, founded by husband-and-wife team Dan and Lana Wright. All-beef hot dogs made locally by Avril-Bleh & Sons with creative toppings including the Croque Madame (béchamel, black forest ham, poached egg on brioche) and Mexico City (guacamole, chipotle crema, bacon, queso fresco, tortilla strips). Full menu features Nashville hot chicken sandwich, gyros, burgers, and house-made falafel. Duck fat fries, truffle fries with harissa aioli, and poutine with local cheese curds and braised short rib gravy. Featured on Cooking Channel's "The Best Thing I Ever Ate." Airy, spacious dining room with outdoor patio in Summit Park.

### Seviche A Latin Restaurant
Chef-owner Anthony Lamas has been putting Louisville on the culinary map since 2005 with his Nuevo Latino cuisine. A four-time James Beard Award semifinalist and Food Network's Extreme Chef winner, Lamas blends his Mexican and Puerto Rican heritage with locally sourced Southern ingredients. All seafood follows Monterey Bay Aquarium's sustainable guidelines. The seasonal patio along Bardstown Road is among the city's best. Known for ceviches, churrascos, and creative cocktails.
$$$

### Sherrilli's Pizzeria
Local pizzeria known for thin-crust pizza baked in fire-bricked ovens, featuring a lunch buffet and menu items including spaghetti, wings, and soft pretzels with warm cheese. Operating with the tagline "Squarely the Best," Sherrilli's offers dine-in, delivery, and takeout with affordable prices and a cozy atmosphere.
$

### Shift Restaurant & Bar - Batesville
Shift Restaurant & Bar offers a welcoming dining experience in Bright, Indiana, featuring a locally-driven menu of contemporary American favorites and pub classics, including burgers, tacos, and unique brunch meals in a casual, heart-warming setting. With a full bar, seasonal outdoor seating, and entertainment like live music, it’s a go-to spot for gatherings with family and friends. Diners appreciate the friendly service, quality comfort food, and relaxed atmosphere that make it a reliable neighborhood restaurant and bar.
$$

### Shift Restaurant & Bar - Bright
Shift Restaurant & Bar offers a welcoming dining experience in Bright, Indiana, featuring a locally-driven menu of contemporary American favorites and pub classics, including burgers, tacos, and unique brunch meals in a casual, heart-warming setting. With a full bar, seasonal outdoor seating, and entertainment like live music, it’s a go-to spot for gatherings with family and friends. Diners appreciate the friendly service, quality comfort food, and relaxed atmosphere that make it a reliable neighborhood restaurant and bar.
$$

### Shiners On the Levee
BBQ, live music, and moonshine destination in the heart of Newport offering mouthwatering BBQ in a cozy, welcoming atmosphere with friendly staff and diverse menu for leisurely dinners, quick lunches, or solo meals at the bar. Features newly renovated speakeasy with one-of-a-kind moonshine tasting experience perfect for groups and private events, creating a relaxed setting where laughter flows freely alongside great food, music, and conversation on the levee.
$$

### Sidecar Bar + Kitchen
Mid-century modern bar and restaurant inside The Hotel Rambler (Tapestry Collection by Hilton), opened October 2025. Nostalgic American diner fare with modern twists—Grippo's Fried Chicken with jalapeño corn waffles, Cincy Smash Patty, Sriracha Teriyaki Steak. Handcrafted cocktails like the Sidecar Old Fashioned. Sleek 1950s-inspired dining room with soft lighting; all-season patio with firepits and TVs. Open to non-hotel guests.
$$

### Six Hundred Downtown
Owned by six-time World Pizza Champion Brittany Saxton, who purchased the restaurant in 2023 after 13+ years in the industry. Named for the 600-degree temperature of their old-world brick ovens. Located in a beautifully renovated former JC Penney building with restored stamped metal ceilings and views into the open kitchen. Dough made in-house daily, local farm-raised products including Blue Jacket Dairy feta cheese. Over 100,000 unique customers annually. Wine room with stone walls for private events.
$$

### Smokin' This and That BBQ
Back-to-back Best of NKY BBQ winner (2017 & 2018), Smokin' This and That brings authentic Southern barbecue to Florence with old-school cherry and hickory wood smoking techniques that make sauce optional—pitmasters Guy and Mandy Cummins' secret dry rub creates fall-off-the-bone ribs, brisket, and pulled pork so tender it'll land in your lap. Since starting in a backyard kitchen in 2013, this family-run community hub (now celebrating 10+ years and planning a second location) has become legendary for signature creations like the BBQ Parfait (layered meat, beans, and Miss Mandy's house-made slaw) and BBQ tacos with secret avocado sauce, all served in a welcoming space that offers military and first responder discounts and proves the best days are spent with family and good food.
$$

### Sneaky Pete's
A Fairfield neighborhood bar and grill since 2007, when it transformed from Double D'z Tavern into Sneaky Pete's. This is NOT connected to the Birmingham, Alabama hot dog chain of the same name—it's a completely independent local establishment. Long-time managers Matt "Chew" and Dalton have cultivated a loyal following with great happy hours, pool tables, a patio, live music on weekends, and classic bar fare including wings, fish sandwiches, potato skins, and grouper bites. TVs throughout for sports viewing, TouchTunes jukebox, and a welcoming atmosphere where regulars feel like family.
$

### Sotto
An intimate, subterranean Italian dining experience set beneath the streets of downtown Cincinnati, known for its candlelit atmosphere and unhurried pacing. The menu centers on house-made pastas, traditional Italian preparations, and thoughtfully sourced ingredients, designed for lingering over multiple courses rather than rushing through a meal. With a focus on warmth, conversation, and timeless technique, the space naturally lends itself to date nights, celebrations, and evenings where the setting is as memorable as what’s on the plate.
$$$

### Spare Time Grill
Family-owned classic American diner in an iconic 1950s building opened in 1958 and revived by the Copley family in 2024; serves breakfast and lunch featuring goetta, eggs, biscuits and gravy, hash browns, the signature Spare Burger (similar to Big Boy), burgers with crinkle-cut fries, Philly cheesesteaks, wings, pickle fries, onion rings, chicken tenders, and soft-serve ice cream served from the front window; known for homemade cream pies.
$

### Speakeasy Ramen
Ohio's best-kept secret hiding in plain sight. Kim Frazier—Springfield native—bought the former Nifty 50's Bar in 2018, chasing a lifelong dream of owning a restaurant. After a year building out the kitchen, she brought in Executive Chef Clayton Horrighs, whose pan-Asian expertise spans Japan, Vietnam, China, and Korea. When the neighborhood regulars weren't thrilled with ramen replacing their dive bar, Frazier hosted a soft opening for friends—and social media did the rest. Now people drive two, three hours for what Yelp voted best ramen in Ohio. The cozy 800-square-foot interior keeps the dive bar charm; the front patio is bigger than the dining room. Signature Tonkotsu ramen, JFC tacos, legendary shrimp rangoons. Local art on the walls, Ohio beers on tap. A five-star dive bar.
$$

### Stella Bleu Bistro
Self-described as 'casual, fine dining' with steak, seafood, and global influences—Italian, French, South American, Asian. Executive Chef Darin Mitchell grew up in Springfield, graduated first in his class at Scottsdale Culinary Institute. Cornerstone of downtown Springfield's restaurant revival.
$$$

### Stone Tavern
Reopened in 2024, this revived neighborhood tavern brings new life to a historic Hamilton building that has served many roles over the decades, including its original run as The Stone Tavern from 1936 to 1972. Today, it offers a relaxed gathering place with craft cocktails, cold draft beer, and a menu that goes beyond typical bar food, blending pub favorites with traditional British dishes like shepherd’s pie, bangers and mash, and fish and chips. Built by hand and run with intention, it feels rooted in community, history, and the simple idea of creating a place where people can come together and unwind.
$$
